summary:
Round 1, TEST review. Every claim below was MEASURED in an issued tree (test-reviewer.6yI5kEsQ) by mutating and running :sequencer:test; nothing here is reasoned from reading.

WHAT THE TEST DOES CATCH. Full revert of the per-pod allocator (leader seq -> `commits`, zombie seq -> `zombieWrites`) fails with exactly the claimed red record: "seed 1 reissued pod1#0 for seg/zombie-23 after seg/2 -- dedup on this pair would suppress a real commit", expected "seg/zombie-23" but was "seg/2", at CommitProtocolSimulationFlushSeqTest.java:59. Both PARTIAL reverts are also killed at the same line, and each by seed 1: leader-only-reverted and zombie-only-reverted both fail, so neither path is carried by the other. Per-pod-but-on-SUCCESS (read `getOrDefault` before the attempt, `merge` after `commits++`/`zombieWrites++`) is killed too, with a different trace -- "seed 1 reissued pod1#5 for seg/24 after seg/zombie-..." -- so the per-ATTEMPT half of the criterion is genuinely pinned.

DETECTION MARGIN. Under a full revert, 7 of the 30 swept seeds trip the assertion (1, 7, 10, 17, 18, 21, 29), first at seed 1. The range is not thin and it matches the two sibling sweeps in CommitProtocolSimulationTest, so 0..29 needs no further defence.

GUARDS THAT BIND. `issuedCount > landed` (line 65) is not decorative: moving both `issued.add` calls to AFTER their `commit` (record on success only) makes it fail with "175 to be greater than 175". `issuedCount` positive (line 63) fails at rounds=0 ("0 to be greater than 0"). `pods` size (line 67) fails at pods=1.

TWO MUTATIONS SURVIVE, both against the row's own stated criterion, and both fixable inside CommitProtocolSimulation.java without touching the assertion. They are the findings below. I also measured that the WHOLE :sequencer: suite is green under the first of them, so nothing else in the repo covers for it.

findings.title: The Issued triple is built from sibling locals, not from the CommitRequest that is sent, so what the test reads can diverge from what `commit` receives
findings.surviving_mutation: Leave both `issued.add(new Issued(...))` lines EXACTLY as staged and change only the second argument of the two `new CommitRequest(...)` calls back to the fleet-global counters: line 210 `new CommitRequest(zombiePod, zombieWrites, zombieSeg, ...)` and line 224 `new CommitRequest(leaderPod, commits, leaderSeg, ...)`. MEASURED: `./gradlew :sequencer:test --tests CommitProtocolSimulationFlushSeqTest` -> BUILD SUCCESSFUL, and the ENTIRE `:sequencer:test` suite -> BUILD SUCCESSFUL. The driver is once again issuing `(pod1, 0)` for two different segments to the sequencer, and every test in the module is green.
findings.failure_scenario: The test is the only thing in the repo that pins `flushSeq` issuance, and it reads `result.issued()` -- a parallel record the driver keeps -- rather than anything derived from the `CommitRequest` actually handed to `commit`. Today the two agree only because four adjacent lines happen to use the same locals; nothing enforces it. A later edit to the commit call (a bad merge, an incomplete revert, a refactor that reintroduces a counter) leaves this test green while the harness reissues exactly the pairs M4.10's dedup keys on -- so M4.10 would be built and 'verified' against a model that lies in precisely the way this row exists to stop, and the M4.27 shape the driver comment at line 125-127 and the test javadoc at lines 28-31 both explicitly claim to have escaped ('a test reads what the driver actually sent') would be back, one indirection out. The fix is mechanical and removes the drift surface entirely: construct the request first and record from its own accessors -- `var req = new CommitRequest(leaderPod, nextFlushSeq.merge(leaderPod, 1L, Long::sum) - 1, leaderSeg, counts(...)); issued.add(new Issued(req.podId(), req.flushSeq(), req.segmentKey())); leader.commit(req);` -- and the same for the zombie. `CommitRequest` is a record, so `podId()`, `flushSeq()` and `segmentKey()` already exist; after that, no mutation of the value sent to `commit` can survive.

findings.title: PER POD -- half the row's stated criterion -- has no assertion that would fail without it; a single fleet-wide per-attempt counter passes
findings.surviving_mutation: Key the allocator on a constant instead of the pod: replace `nextFlushSeq.merge(leaderPod, 1L, Long::sum)` (line 222) and `nextFlushSeq.merge(zombiePod, 1L, Long::sum)` (line 208) with `nextFlushSeq.merge("shared", 1L, Long::sum)`. MEASURED: BUILD SUCCESSFUL. Uniqueness of `(podId, flushSeq)` is trivially satisfied by any monotone fleet-wide counter, because such a counter never emits a number twice at all -- so the assertion at line 55-59 cannot distinguish per-pod from fleet-wide.
findings.failure_scenario: The backlog row's headline is 'MAKE THE SIMULATION ISSUE flushSeq PER POD, PER ATTEMPT'. Per-attempt is pinned (the on-SUCCESS variant dies); per-pod is not, so testing.md rule 13 is unmet for the first half. The aggravating factor is that line 67's own description -- 'one pod cannot show a per-POD allocator is per-pod' -- reads as though this assertion establishes per-pod allocation. It does not: it only establishes that more than one pod NAME appears among the issued triples, which the shared counter also satisfies. A reader auditing this file later would credit it with a property it never checked. Consequence downstream: M4.10 reasons with `lastAppliedFlushSeq` PER POD, and a harness whose per-pod sequences are sparse and coupled to other pods' activity is not the field behaviour that row is being designed against, while this test reports that it is. MEASURED strengthening that holds on the staged code: across seeds 0..29 at ROUGH, every pod's issued flushSeq sequence is exactly 0,1,2,...,n-1 -- 0 non-dense pods out of the whole sweep -- so asserting per-pod density from zero (or, more narrowly and without restating the increment, that within a single seed two DISTINCT pods each issue flushSeq 0) passes on the fix and kills the shared allocator immediately.

findings.title: The javadoc's justification for the faulted profile is false; the defect is reached at CLEAN too
findings.surviving_mutation: Revert the allocator AND switch ROUGH to `FaultInjectingStore.Faults.none()`. MEASURED: still fails -- 'seed 0 reissued pod0#0 for seg/zombie-31 after seg/1'. Conversely, switching only the profile to CLEAN on the staged (fixed) code leaves the test green, `issuedCount > landed` included.
findings.failure_scenario: Line 38 says 'The defect needs a FAILED commit, so the faulted profile is what reaches it.' A failed commit is not the same as an INJECTED fault: a fenced zombie's `commit` throws `IOException` with no faults configured at all, which is why the reissue reproduces at CLEAN. So the `issuedCount > landed` guard at line 65 binds 'some attempt failed', not 'an injected fault failed a commit' -- weaker than the sentence implies, though still binding (it killed the record-on-success mutation). No hole today: ROUGH is a superset and the assertion is correct either way. Recorded because the sentence is the stated reason for the profile choice, and a future hand trusting it would think the profile is load-bearing when it is not -- the same 'prose describing the test is stronger than the test' failure this review exists to catch, at minor scale.

findings.title: No @Timeout on a 30-seed simulation sweep, unlike the sibling that runs the same workload
findings.surviving_mutation: Not a coverage gap -- no production mutation survives because of it. MEASURED runtime today: 1.03s and 1.02s over two runs.
findings.failure_scenario: `CommitProtocolSimulationTest` carries `@Timeout(value = 120, threadMode = SEPARATE_THREAD)` for the same 30-seed, 120-round, 3-pod sweep; this new class carries none. The driver's own comment at CommitProtocolSimulation.java:151-159 records a real stall in this harness ('the simulation DEADLOCKS ... reported no violations about a cluster that had stopped'). If that class of bug returns, the sibling sweep fails in 120s and this one hangs the suite, which is a worse failure mode than a red test and is invisible to the suite-time gate until it has already cost a session. One annotation.
